primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Congenital short QT syndrome due to gain-of-function repolarizing potassium current
mechanism: Gain-of-function variants in repolarizing potassium channels can increase outward potassium current during the ventricular action potential, abbreviating action-potential duration and the effective refractory period. This promotes reentry and predisposes to atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias and sudden death.
vignette: A 19-year-old man is evaluated after an unexplained syncopal episode during rest. His father died suddenly at age 28 years. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart. Repeated electrocardiograms show a markedly abbreviated QT interval with tall, narrow-based T waves. Genetic testing identifies a gain-of-function variant in KCNH2.
lead: Which of the following electrophysiologic changes most directly explains this patient's increased risk of tachyarrhythmia?
correct: Increased outward repolarizing potassium current shortens ventricular action-potential duration and the effective refractory period
distractors: Reduced outward potassium current prolongs phase 3 repolarization and promotes early afterdepolarizations
Persistent inward sodium current prolongs the action potential and increases dispersion of repolarization
Reduced sodium-channel availability slows right ventricular conduction and produces phase 2 reentry
Reduced inward rectifier potassium current prolongs terminal repolarization and produces prominent U waves
distractor_notes: Reduced repolarizing potassium current is a classic mechanism of congenital long-QT syndromes, not short-QT syndrome.
Persistent inward sodium current also prolongs repolarization and is associated with long-QT phenotypes.
Reduced sodium current is associated with Brugada/conduction phenotypes. The supplied KCNH2 gain-of-function variant instead accelerates repolarization.
Loss of inward rectifier potassium current is associated with Andersen-Tawil phenotypes and QT/U-wave abnormalities rather than abbreviated repolarization.
key_expl: Short QT syndrome is an inherited channelopathy characterized by abnormally abbreviated repolarization and susceptibility to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. Gain-of-function variants in potassium-channel genes such as KCNH2 increase repolarizing outward current, shortening ventricular action-potential duration and refractory periods. Short refractory periods facilitate reentrant arrhythmias.
objective: Explain how gain-of-function repolarizing potassium-channel variants cause short QT syndrome by shortening action-potential duration and refractory period.
